balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

postpaidNetAdds.title: Postpaid net additions
postpaidNetAdds.content:
Postpaid net adds is new postpaid connections less losses in the period; the phone-only line strips out tablets, watches and other connected devices to isolate the core subscription business.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: postpaid phone adds are the metric wireless carriers are judged on every quarter -- the UScellular acquisition (closed August 2025) and the 5G/FWA pitch to rural and underserved households are both aimed at keeping this line positive relative to AT&T and Verizon.

What to watch:

  • Total postpaid adds diverging from phone adds (device vs. connected-device growth)
  • Seasonality around promotional periods and iPhone launches

churn.title: Postpaid phone and prepaid churn
churn.content:
Churn is the percentage of the subscriber base that disconnects in the period. Postpaid phone churn is the carrier-quality signal; prepaid churn runs several times higher because prepaid customers have no contract and are more price-sensitive.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: postpaid phone churn near 0.8-0.9% is among the lowest in the US wireless industry and underpins the ARPA growth guidance -- a sustained uptick would signal competitive or network-quality pressure, including from the UScellular integration.

What to watch:

  • Postpaid phone churn creeping above ~1.0%
  • Prepaid churn trend as Metro by T-Mobile competes with cable MVNOs (Spectrum Mobile, Xfinity Mobile)

customerBase.title: Customer base
customerBase.content:
Total customers is the full subscriber base; postpaid and prepaid connections split it by plan type (postpaid also includes non-phone devices such as tablets and FWA lines in some periods).

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: postpaid has grown roughly 4x faster than prepaid since FY2021, including the step-up from the UScellular close in Q3 2025 -- prepaid (mainly Metro by T-Mobile) is the slower, more price-competitive segment.

What to watch:

  • Postpaid share of the base rising over time (mix shift toward higher-value plans)
  • Gaps in a given period mean the metric was not separately disclosed that quarter

arpaArpu.title: Postpaid ARPA and prepaid ARPU
arpaArpu.content:
ARPA (average revenue per account) is postpaid service revenue divided by accounts, capturing multi-line household and business pricing; ARPU is revenue per individual prepaid connection.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: management raised FY2026 postpaid ARPA growth guidance to ~3.5% (from 2.5-3%) after Q3 2026 ARPA grew 4% YoY to $155.73 -- plan mix (Go5G Plus/Next), price increases and bundled perks (Netflix, Apple One) are the drivers.

What to watch:

  • ARPA growth outpacing or lagging the ~3.5% FY2026 target
  • Prepaid ARPU, which has drifted down since FY2021 as Metro competes on price

broadbandNetAdds.title: FWA and fiber broadband net adds
broadbandNetAdds.content:
FWA net adds are new fixed wireless access broadband connections sold over excess 5G network capacity; fiber net adds come from the capital-light 50/50 fiber joint ventures (Lumos, Metronet, i3 Broadband, and GoNetspeed/Greenlight once closed).

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: broadband is T-Mobile's biggest stated growth driver beyond core wireless, targeting 18-19 million total broadband customers (3-4 million of them fiber) by 2030; FWA alone already passed 8 million connections by FY2025.

What to watch:

  • FWA net-add deceleration as network capacity in dense markets gets reallocated to mobile traffic
  • Fiber net adds scaling up as more JVs close and consolidate (data only starts Q3 2025)

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For T-Mobile US, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
